transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 mins
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Sofia Chen (Redwood SE), Mark Ellis (Acme Lead Eng), Priya Nair (Acme Platform Eng), Jordan Lee (CTO)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood inference, i'm the account exec, and with me is Sofia who's our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Mark: good, thanks. thanks for setting this up. we have about 45 minutes, we want to focus on the SDKs, auth, and a quick demo of the python/typescript quickstart.
[00:14] Sofia: great, we'll keep it practical - i'll show a short python quickstart, then typescript, and we can dive into auth and deployment questions. if we run over we can follow up.
[00:22] Jordan: perfect. main constraints: we need sub-200ms p99 for short chat calls and we care about on-prem options for regulated datasets.
[00:30] Sofia: totally, we'll cover hosted vs dedicated vs private and what that means for latency and ROIs.
[00:36] --- quick contextual questions ---
[00:40] Alex: can you remind us what your current stack looks like? are you using OpenAI or something internal?
[00:44] Priya: we've been using OpenAI for prototyping, a mix of GPT-4 for higher quality and local smaller models for offline tasks. infra is mostly GCP, and we have a KMS for keys.
[00:55] Alex: good, so you'll be familiar with API keys and the general pattern. we'll show both API key auth and SSO options, and note how KMS integrates for private deployments.
[01:05] --- Python quickstart demo (Sofia) ---
[01:06] Sofia: i'll paste the commands, sorry i might read it out loud: pip install redwood-inference (note: package name is 'redwood-inference'), then export REDWOOD_API_KEY="sk-REDACTED" or set it in your env manager. example snippet: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate('summarize this report').
[01:29] Mark: quick q - is the python lib sync-only or has streaming callbacks?
[01:33] Sofia: it supports streaming via an iterator or async callbacks, we show an example in the repo. streaming behavior is same across hosted and dedicated.
[01:41] Jordan: how are model variants exposed? can we pin a model version?
[01:44] Sofia: yes, you can specify model: "rw/gpt-2-large:2026-05-01" in the request or pin in the console for routes. we also surface quantized variants for cost savings. sometimes the transcript shows the model names slightly off - docs have canonical names.
[02:00] --- TypeScript quickstart ---
[02:02] Sofia: npm i @redwood/inference, then const { Redwood } = require('@redwood/inference'); const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); client.chat.create({ model: 'rw/llama-quant', messages: [...] }).then(...).
[02:20] Priya: do you have first-party SDKs for node streams? we need to pipe partial tokens to our websocket layer.
[02:25] Sofia: yes, the node SDK exposes an event emitter for tokens and the examples show piping to sockets.
[02:31] Alex: also we have a short sample repo with express + websocket patterns, i'll share the link.
[02:38] Mark: any gotchas for serverless vs k8s?
[02:42] Sofia: serverless can be fine for low QPS but for predictable throughput you typically use Dedicated capacity or run in a VPC/private. caching and batching are big wins to lower costs with p99 targets.
[02:54] --- Auth discussion ---
[02:55] Alex: on auth: API keys are simplest for quickstarts. for production you can use SSO/SAML provisioning and short-lived keys via our control plane; for private deployments you can integrate with customer KMS/HSM to rotate keys.
[03:10] Priya: we use GCP KMS - how deep is the integration?
[03:14] Sofia: for Redwood Private we support customer-managed keys and integrations with GCP KMS, AWS KMS, and HSM. for hosted customers we store encrypted keys and support bring-your-own-key via a KMS bridge in enterprise plans.
[03:27] Jordan: audit logs and role-based access are critical, we can't have broad developer keys.
[03:31] Alex: yes, RBAC, audit logs, and per-route tokens are supported. we'll include the SOC2 summary in the pack.
[03:38] --- Environment setup & quickstarts details ---
[03:40] Sofia: quick checklist for engineers: 1) pip/npm install SDK, 2) set REDWOOD_API_KEY, 3) run sample prompt set to verify latency, 4) use small batch sizes for low latency. dev note: default batcher may coalesce requests, you can tune max latency window.
[03:58] Mark: can you show the sample env file?
[04:00] Sofia: yes, .env example: REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxx; REDWOOD_DEFAULT_MODEL=rw/llama-instruct; REDWOOD_REGION=us-west1. for typescript: export REDWOOD_API_KEY, then node index.js.
[04:18] Priya: we'd like a docker example too - run the sdk inside a container and set env at deploy time.
[04:22] Sofia: we have a small dockerfile in the repo, i'll point it out.
[04:26] --- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs ---
[04:28] Alex: hosted is fastest to start and cost-effective for bursty, Dedicated gives guaranteed capacity and lower per-token cost at commit, Private is for strict compliance and on-prem needs but has longer lead times.
[04:41] Jordan: what's the bootstrap time for Private? we have air-gapped requirements for some workloads.
[04:45] Sofia: private on-prem typically 4-8 weeks depending on procurement and network approvals; VPC deployments are faster. also note we support hybrid routing so sensitive inference can go to private pools while other requests use hosted.
[05:02] Mark: how do we measure cost impact of quantization vs latency?
[05:06] Sofia: we provide Optimize suggestions and estimated unit economics in the console; our SE team can run a short eval to show token cost and latency delta for q4_0 vs fp16 on their sample prompts.
[05:18] --- Technical deep dive questions from Mark ---
[05:20] Mark: in python, how much boilerplate to resume kv cache across requests? we want session continuity across sharded engines.
[05:27] Sofia: we expose session tokens and a cache id; in dedicated setups we can pin KV caches; the SDK surfaces checkpoint/resume helpers. latency varies by model and sequence length. (note: transcription occasionally garbles exact function names).
[05:44] Priya: are there any rate limits on tokens for dedicated?
[05:47] Alex: dedicated customers can configure quotas and we surface per-route rate limits; defaults are more relevant to hosted.
[05:53] --- Objections and procurement topics ---
[05:55] Jordan: procurement will ask for standard SLAs and export controls; also need pricing for a 12-month committed capacity.
[06:03] Alex: we'll include a committed pricing sheet and SLA language, and we can introduce legal contacts in the next step.
[06:09] --- Misc transcript artifacts / crosstalk ---
[06:10] Speaker 1: mm-hmm
[06:12] Mark: sorry if i interrupt, i just want to make sure the streaming works with our websocket fanout
[06:17] Sofia: yes, we do that pattern in the example.
[06:20] --- Recap and explicit next steps ---
[06:21] Alex: recap - Sofia will send the quickstart repo and docker example, i'll send pricing + SOC2 summary, Mark will provide sample prompts and token distribution. if those look good we'll schedule a pilot kick-off in two weeks.
[06:36] Jordan: sounds good.
[06:38] Alex: thanks everyone. i'll follow up with calendar invite and materials.
[06:42] Mark: thanks.

[end of transcript]

Notes: transcript includes occasional mis-attributions and small transcription errors as typical of Fireflies exports. Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.ai/docs/sdk-quickstart , repo link (shared in chat), pricing deck (to be emailed).
